final_proof:
Let \(I_n\) denote the \(n\times n\) identity matrix. Recall that \(B\) is a left inverse of \(A\) precisely when \(BA=I_n\), while it is a right inverse of \(A\) precisely when \(AB=I_n\).

Suppose first that \(BA=I_n\). Regard \(A\) and \(B\) as linear maps from \(\mathbb F^n\) to itself. If \(x\in\mathbb F^n\) satisfies \(Ax=0\), then
\[
x=I_nx=(BA)x=B(Ax)=0.
\]
Thus \(A\) is injective. By the rank-nullity theorem, an injective linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space \(\mathbb F^n\) is surjective. Consequently, for each \(y\in\mathbb F^n\), there is an \(x\in\mathbb F^n\) such that \(y=Ax\). For such an \(x\), associativity of matrix multiplication and \(BA=I_n\) give
\[
(AB)y=(AB)(Ax)=A(BA)x=AI_nx=Ax=y.
\]
Since this holds for every \(y\in\mathbb F^n\), the linear map represented by \(AB\) is the identity, and hence \(AB=I_n\). Therefore every left inverse of a square matrix over a field is also a right inverse.

Conversely, suppose that \(AB=I_n\). If \(Bx=0\), then
\[
x=I_nx=(AB)x=A(Bx)=0,
\]
so \(B\) is injective and therefore, again by rank-nullity, surjective. Given \(y\in\mathbb F^n\), choose \(x\) with \(y=Bx\). Then
\[
(BA)y=(BA)(Bx)=B(AB)x=BI_nx=Bx=y.
\]
Thus \(BA=I_n\), so every right inverse is also a left inverse. In particular, whenever a square matrix over a field has a one-sided inverse, that inverse is two-sided.

Moreover, if \(L\) is any left inverse and \(R\) any right inverse of \(A\), then
\[
L=LI_n=L(AR)=(LA)R=I_nR=R.
\]
Thus left and right inverses are equal.

The problem's last sentence literally says that a right inverse is a right inverse, which is immediate from the definition. The symmetric assertion evidently intended there—namely, that a right inverse is also a left inverse—is the converse proved above.
